title: When prayer feels empty
hookLine: keep praying through dry seasons; the practice holds you
tomorrow: a scary thought about God shows up. does that mean faith is gone?

lines: A PRAYER LIKE A GROCERY LIST.
cards: The party's over. Chairs folded, dishes stacked, the house too quiet. The next morning you stand to pray and it feels like reading a grocery list.
A report in Sahih al-Bukhari gives an answer that sounds almost too plain. 'A'isha passed on what the Prophet ﷺ taught: the deeds most loved by God are the ones done regularly, even if they're small.

teach.b: Not the most intense. The most steady. That's the quiet logic of praying anyway: the feeling comes and goes, and the prayer keeps its time.
The Qur'an doesn't pretend it's easy.
In Pickthall's words: "Seek help in patience and prayer; and truly it is hard save for the humble-minded." Hard, it says, out loud.
And when the time for prayer came, the Prophet would say to Bilal, who gave the call: give us rest by it. Rest, not a chore to get through.
On a dry morning the rest may be nothing more than showing up and standing where you always stand. The practice holds you when the feeling won't.

teach.h: A WEEK OF FRIENDS AND FAMILY.
teach.b: Now the week, quickly. A perfume seller: choose friends well. An angel on the road: visits for his sake.
Hot ashes and a helper: reconnect. Abraham's calf: honor guests. Abu Quhafa, seated: care for elders.
A race and a rematch: one household.
And this morning, a prayer that felt like nothing, prayed anyway.

how: Muslims keep the daily prayers at their times whether or not they feel moved, and teachers point to the hadith on small, steady deeds for dry seasons.

games.q: what does “when prayer feels empty” mean?
o: a prayer said only when someone has died
praying through dry days when it feels like nothing
skipping prayer until the feeling comes back

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: seek help in patience and prayer

s: a prayer only counts if you feel something during it
the deeds most loved by God are the steady ones, even if small.
the Qur'an admits that prayer is hard, except for the humble-minded
the Prophet spoke of prayer as a rest: give us rest by it
his words to Bilal when the time for prayer came.

games.q: your friend quit the gym because it 'doesn't feel good anymore.' she asks if prayer works the same way: wait for the spark, then go back?
o: yes; worship without the feeling is just going through the motions.
no; the hadith loves the steady deed, and the Qur'an admits prayer is hard.
only if she prays twice as long once the spark comes back.
games.why: the deeds most loved are the regular ones, even if small, and 2:45 says plainly that prayer is hard. the feeling isn't the test; the steadiness is.

practice: Stand, or sit up straight, the way you might at the start of a prayer, and let your hands rest. Keep that posture for the whole time, even if your mind wanders and nothing in particular happens.
The body keeps the place while the feeling catches up.

wordCard.voice: When prayer feels empty: the dry seasons, when nothing moves. The answer here is steadiness; the prayer keeps its time.

orig.note: Arabic: 'give us rest by it'; the Prophet's words to Bilal about prayer.

carryVoice: First line of the hard days: pray anyway, because small and steady is what's loved. See you next week.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 ('A'isha: the deeds most loved by God are the most regular, even if small)
